items.title: IRGC Navy intercepts two vessels in southern waters of Hormuz
items.summary: IRGC Navy intercepts two vessels in southern waters of Hormuz Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Friday that it halted two tankers in the southern waters of the Strait of Hormuz after they attempted to pass through an unauthorised route. In a statement, the IRGC Navy said the vessels, one in the eastern and the other in the western part of the strait, had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and ignored several radio warnings. It accused the US military of supporting the attempted passage and blamed what it called hostile US actions, along with the vessels’ disregard for Iranian regulations, for the incidents and fires aboard the ships. The IRGC Navy also said another vessel that caught fire in the southern waters of the strait on Thursday night had sunk.

items.title: Old News: After 26-year rule, Shah of Iran crowns himself ‘King of Kings’
items.summary: Old News is a new initiative by Amwaj.media to connect the past to the present. Through “reporting” on pivotal moments in history, we aim to provide a richer backdrop for current dynamics in the region. The story: Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi has crowned himself Iran’s “King of Kings,” and his wife as Empress. The event took place at a lavish ceremony in Tehran's Golestan Palace, 26 years after becoming head of state. Observers say Pahlavi has delayed his coronation to await the birth of a male heir, and to initiate enough progress and reform in Iran to legitimize his rule. The coronation has drawn national and international praise for reforms implemented as part of the Shah’s “White Revolution,” though he is also facing domestic criticism for his policies and autocratic rule. The coverage: Pahlavi crowned himself Shahanshah , “King of Kings” of the Imperial State of Iran, on Oct. 26 1967—marking his 48th birthday.

items.summary: During a meeting last week with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, Russian President Vladimir Putin offered to help broker a deal to end the U.S.-Iran war. The proposal — the latest in a series of recent Russian offers to act as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran — has a certain logic to it. While the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran has brought Russia some economic gains through rising energy prices, Moscow fears further escalation and spillover across the Persian Gulf and parts of the former Soviet space. Russia is also one of Iran’s closest partners and one of the world’s leading exporters of enriched uranium, meaning that it could help break the impasse over domestic Iranian nuclear enrichment. Yet Moscow will struggle to gain Western and Gulf Arab acceptance as a mediator, particularly amid the Ukraine conflict and heightened threat perceptions of Iran in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) while Russia is increasingly aligned with Iran. items.title: What the Midterms Mean for U.S. Foreign Policy
items.summary: If the polls are right, Democrats will retake at least one chamber of Congress in the U.S. midterms. And with voters focused on the cost of living, foreign policy is an unusually impactful driver at the ballot box: Tariffs have raised the price of everyday goods, and the war with Iran has sent gas prices soaring. How might Democrats use their new power over spending and oversight to challenge Trump’s agenda in his final two years in office? How will allies and adversaries read the results? Susan Glasser, a staff writer at the New Yorker and former editor in chief of Foreign Policy, will join FP Live to break down what the midterms mean for congressional power and for America’s standing in the world.

items.title: The Legacy of Reykjavik and the Future of U.S.–Russia Nuclear Relations
items.summary: On 11-12 October 1986, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met in Reykjavik, Iceland, hoping to achieve a groundbreaking agreement on controlling the world’s most dangerous weapons. While the summit yielded no agreement, it set in motion arms control negotiations tracks, held up the promise of nuclear disarmament, and contributed to the transformation of relations between two Cold War ach-adversaries. Forty years on, what lessons does Reykjavik hold for arms control, disarmament, and great power relations? To discuss the legacy of Reykjavik, Project on Managing the Atom (MTA) is honored to welcome Pavel Palazhchenko, former interpreter of Mikhail Gorbachev and an ambassador of the Gorbachev Foundation, David Holloway, Professor Emeritus of Stanford University and author of the International History of Nuclear Weapons, Matthew Bunn, Professor at Harvard Kennedy School, and Carol Saivetz, Senior Fellow at MIT Security Studies Program, with Mariana Budjeryn, MTA associate and a senior researcher at MIT as moderator.
